'''Merav Opher''' is a professor of [[astronomy]] at [[Boston University]] known for her work on the [[heliosphere]], the cocoon formed by the wind emanated from the Sun as it travels in the Galaxy. In 2021 she was named a William Bentinck-Smith Fellow at the [[Harvard Radcliffe Institute]].

==Education and career==
Opher was born in Israel and lived there until 1978 when she moved to Brazil with her parents.<ref name=":3">{{Citation|title=Merav Opher reads "One Art" by Elizabeth Bishop (Favorite Poem Project)| date=8 October 2018 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yi092jHpKbc|language=en|access-date=2021-12-17}}</ref> In 1992 and 1998, Opher received her B.S. in physics and her Ph.D. in physics and astronomy from the [[University of São Paulo]].<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=Efeitos de plasma no universo primordial.|trans-title=Plasma effects in the primordial universe.|date=1998|publisher=University of Sao Paulo|language=Portuguese|first=Merav|last=Opher|oclc = 55913904}}</ref> Following her Ph.D., Opher was a postdoctoral investigator at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] from 1999 until 2001. She was a Caltech Scholar at NASA's [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]] and at [[University of Michigan]] from 2001-2004. She was on the faculty of [[George Mason University]] from 2005 until 2010, at which point she moved to [[Boston University]], where she was promoted to professor in 2020.<ref name="Merav Opher CV">{{cite web|title=Merav Opher|url=http://people.bu.edu/mopher/CV-merav.pdf|access-date=12 March 2021|website=BU}}</ref>

Opher is the director of the SHIELD DRIVE Science Center at Boston University, a project funded by NASA that will study the shape of the heliosphere.<ref>{{Cite web|title=People|url=https://shielddrivecenter.com/people/|access-date=2021-12-17|website=SHIELD DRIVE Science Center}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Jahnke|first=Art|date=February 21, 2020|title=Visualizing The Heliosphere, Our Solar System's Protective Bubble|url=https://www.bu.edu/articles/2020/visualizing-the-heliosphere-merav-opher/|access-date=2021-12-17|website=Boston University|language=en}}</ref> She has served on the Space Studies Board at the [[National Academy of Sciences]] which evaluated the progress of space and solar physics.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Committee on the Review of Progress Toward Implementing the Decadal Survey – Solar and Space Physics: A Science for a Technological Society|url=https://www.nap.edu/catalog/25668|title=Progress Toward Implementation of the 2013 Decadal Survey for Solar and Space Physics: A Midterm Assessment|last2=Space Studies Board|last3=Division on Engineering and Physical Sciences|last4=National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine|date=2020-06-29|publisher=National Academies Press|isbn=978-0-309-67127-9|location=Washington, D.C.|doi=10.17226/25668|s2cid=241931425}}</ref>

==Research==
Her research interests include computational and theoretical [[plasma physics]] in space and [[astrophysics]], interaction of the [[Solar System]] with the [[interstellar medium]], [[solar wind]], and shocks in the lower corona, T-Tauri and Solar-Like Stars.<ref name="Merav Opher Bio">{{cite web|title=Merav Opher|url=http://www.bu.edu/csp/profiles/merav-opher/|access-date=12 March 2021|website=BU Center for Space Physics}}</ref> In 2001, Opher began work on the heliosphere while she was a postdoctoral student at the Jet Propulsion lab.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Laskowski|first=Tara|date=2008|title=Past Pluto - The Mason Spirit - George Mason University|url=https://spirit.gmu.edu/archives/spring08/past_pluto.html|access-date=2021-12-17|website=spirit.gmu.edu}}</ref> Her researcher focuses on how the solar wind shapes the heliosphere, the protective atmospheric shield between Earth and the rest of the galaxy, where she has shown the shape of the heliosphere is similar to a croissant and not a comet with a tail as previously thought.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Opher|first1=M.|last2=Drake|first2=J. F.|last3=Swisdak|first3=M.|last4=Zieger|first4=B.|last5=Toth|first5=G.|date=2017-04-11|title=The Twist of the Draped Interstellar Magnetic Field Ahead of the Heliopause: A Magnetic Reconnection Driven Rotational Discontinuity|journal=The Astrophysical Journal|language=en|volume=839|issue=1|pages=L12|doi=10.3847/2041-8213/aa692f|arxiv=1702.06178|bibcode=2017ApJ...839L..12O|s2cid=119088337|issn=2041-8213 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Opher's 2020 paper expanding on the crescent shape of the heliosphere was published in ''[[Nature Astronomy]]'', featured on the cover of the July 2020 issue,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Opher|first1=Merav|last2=Loeb|first2=Abraham|last3=Drake|first3=James|last4=Toth|first4=Gabor|date=2020-07-01|title=A small and round heliosphere suggested by magnetohydrodynamic modelling of pick-up ions|url=http://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-020-1036-0|journal=Nature Astronomy|language=en|volume=4|issue=7|pages=675–683|doi=10.1038/s41550-020-1036-0|bibcode=2020NatAs...4..675O|s2cid=216241125|issn=2397-3366|hdl=2144/40769|hdl-access=free}}</ref> and covered by the media.<ref>{{Cite web|last1=Jean|first1=Celia|last2=Reich|first2=Aaron|date=August 9, 2020|title=Solar system's heliosphere may be croissant-shaped - study|url=https://www.jpost.com/health-science/solar-systems-heliosphere-may-be-croissant-shaped-study-637997|access-date=2021-12-17|website=[[The Jerusalem Post]]|language=en-US |issn=0792-822X}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Crowley|first=James|date=2020-08-11|title=NASA says we all live inside a giant "deflated croissant", yes really|url=https://www.newsweek.com/nasa-data-solar-system-deflated-cocoon-1524373|access-date=2021-12-17|website=Newsweek|language=en}}</ref> In 2021, Opher's research revealed that the stability of the heliosphere originates from the neutral hydrogen particles that interact with the heliosphere.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Opher|first1=M.|last2=Drake|first2=J. F.|last3=Zank|first3=G.|last4=Powell|first4=E.|last5=Shelley|first5=W.|last6=Kornbleuth|first6=M.|last7=Florinski|first7=V.|last8=Izmodenov|first8=V.|last9=Giacalone|first9=J.|last10=Fuselier|first10=S.|last11=Dialynas|first11=K.|date=2021-12-01|title=A Turbulent Heliosheath Driven by the Rayleigh–Taylor Instability|journal=The Astrophysical Journal|volume=922|issue=2|pages=181|doi=10.3847/1538-4357/ac2d2e|bibcode=2021ApJ...922..181O|s2cid=244797589|issn=0004-637X|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Reich|first=Aaron|date=December 5, 2021|title=Neutral hydrogen gives solar system's heliosphere its croissant-shape|url=https://www.jpost.com/science/neutral-hydrogen-gives-solar-systems-heliosphere-its-croissant-shape-study-687891|access-date=2021-12-17|website=[[The Jerusalem Post]]|language=en-US |issn=0792-822X}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Carleton|first=Audrey|date=December 7, 2021|title=A Flaky Croissant-Shaped Bubble Surrounds Our Solar System, Scientists Say|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/a-flaky-croissant-shaped-bubble-surrounds-our-solar-system-scientists-say/|access-date=2021-12-17|website=Vice.com|language=en}}</ref>

Opher has written in ''The Hill'' about the dangers of space tourism for people where she describes the radiation coming through space and the need to better understand how the heliosphere filters this radiation before people can travel safely to other planets.<ref>{{Cite web|first1=Merav|last1=Opher|last2=Ayala|first2=Christine|date=2021-11-27|title=Health risks of space tourism: Is it responsible to send humans to Mars?|url=https://thehill.com/opinion/technology/583245-health-risks-of-space-tourism-is-it-responsible-to-send-humans-to-mars|access-date=2021-12-17|website=TheHill|language=en}}</ref>

As of 2021, Opher's research has been cited more than 4400 times and she has an [[h-index]] of 37.<ref>{{Cite web|title=merav opher|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=KyPxq6sAAAAJ&hl=en|access-date=2021-12-12|website=Google Scholar}}</ref>

==Honors and awards==
In 2008, Opher received an NSF Young Investigator Award,<ref name="Merav Opher Bio" /> a [[Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=White House Announces 2007 Awards for Early Career Scientists and Engineers|url=https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/news/releases/2008/12/20081219-10.html|access-date=2021-12-12|website=georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov}}</ref> and she was named a Kavli Fellow by the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="Merav Opher CV" /> In 2021, Opher was named a William Bentinck-Smith Fellow at the [[Harvard Radcliffe Institute]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Merav Opher|url=https://www.radcliffe.harvard.edu/people/merav-opher|access-date=2021-12-12|website=Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study at Harvard University|language=en}}</ref>
